What You Need to Know Sep 14, 2026 Sep 14, 2026 0 Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save (StatePoint) Respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, is a common respiratory virus that can infect people of all ages. While most people develop mild symptoms, for some, including older adults, it can develop into severe illness. Each year in the United States, up to 180,000 older adults are hospitalized due to RSV. Age, underlying medical conditions and other factors increase the risk of developing severe and even life-threatening illness. That’s why the American Lung Association is launching an educational public health initiative to increase awareness of the virus, the importance of vaccination, and additional prevention methods to help reduce its spread. As part of the campaign, they are answering some commonly asked questions about RSV: How does RSV spread? Like many other respiratory viruses, RSV spreads easily from person to person, with seasonality beginning during the fall and peaking in winter months. The virus spreads through close contact with infected individuals from coughing and sneezing, direct contact with an infected individual, and by touching objects that have the virus on them. Who is most at risk for developing complications? Severe complications from RSV include pneumonia, and the worsening of existing long-term health conditions like asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and congestive heart failure. These complications can lead to a decreased quality of life due to long-lasting symptoms, a diminished ability to carry out daily activities, and a loss of independence. Among adults, those at increased risk include people ages 75 and older, adults with chronic lung or heart disease such as asthma, COPD, interstitial lung disease or congestive heart failure, adults with weakened immune systems, and those living in nursing homes. How can people protect themselves? As of February 2026, only 43% of adults 75 and older and 33% of adults 50-74 with a condition that increases their risk for RSV reported having ever received an RSV vaccine, leaving many eligible adults without vaccination protection. The Lung Association encourages people to speak with their healthcare provider about staying up to date on all respiratory vaccinations to protect their health. RSV, flu and COVID vaccines can be received in the same visit. Who is eligible for RSV vaccination? The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends RSV vaccination for adults 75 and older and for adults ages 50 through 74 who are at high risk of developing severe RSV disease. The best time to get vaccinated is in the late summer or early fall, before the virus spreads widely. However, people can be vaccinated at any time. RSV vaccination is not recommended annually. For adults who have already received an RSV vaccine, no additional doses are needed at this time. What other measures can people take to prevent RSV transmission? In addition to vaccination, the following healthy habits can help reduce the spread of RSV and other respiratory infections: washing hands regularly, covering coughs and sneezes with a tissue, avoiding close contact with people who are ill, staying home when sick, cleaning frequently touched surfaces, improving indoor air quality and wearing a mask when sick or around others who are ill. For more information about RSV prevention and vaccination, visit Lung.org/rsv. RSV is not only common, it can be dangerous. Fortunately, tools are available to protect those at higher risk for serious illness this fall, winter, and beyond. While every respiratory illness season is different, health experts say preparing before illnesses begin circulating widely can help reduce the risk of severe illness and complications. As the respiratory illness season approaches, health care providers are encouraging individuals and families to take preventive steps now, including staying up to date on recommended vaccinations, practicing good hand hygiene and staying home when sick. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), annual flu vaccination is recommended for everyone 6 months and older, with rare exceptions, because influenza viruses change over time and vaccine formulations are updated to help protect against strains expected to circulate each season. "Viruses change from year to year, which is why annual flu and COVID-19 vaccinations remain important," said Bill Johnston, MD, Aspirus Primary Care Provider. "Getting vaccinated in September or October gives your body time to build immunity before respiratory illnesses become more widespread in our communities." Many people assume they can rely on a healthy immune system alone, but vaccination adds an extra layer of protection. While vaccines can’t totally prevent respiratory illness, medical experts note that vaccines can help reduce the severity of illness, lower the risk of hospitalization and decrease the likelihood of serious complications. "Having a healthy immune system is a great start, but vaccines help strengthen those defenses," Johnston said. "Even if someone does become ill, vaccination can help minimize the severity of illness and reduce the chance of hospitalization." Certain groups face a greater risk of serious illness during respiratory virus season. Older adults, infants and young children, people with weakened immune systems and individuals with chronic health conditions such as heart disease, lung disease or diabetes may be more likely to experience complications. Johnston said protecting vulnerable community members requires a collective effort. "There are some groups we especially want to protect, including newborns, older adults and people with weakened immune systems," Johnston said. "When eligible individuals get vaccinated, they help create a layer of protection around those who are most vulnerable." In addition to recommended vaccinations, providers encourage families to practice routine preventive measures throughout the season. These include frequent handwashing, covering coughs and sneezes, cleaning commonly touched surfaces and staying home when sick. Health experts say no single strategy is perfect, but combining multiple prevention measures can help reduce the spread of illness within households, schools, workplaces and communities. "The combination of vaccination, good hand hygiene and thoughtful respiratory etiquette can make a meaningful difference," Johnston said. "Small actions help protect not only you and your family, but also the people around you." As respiratory illness season begins, health professionals emphasize that prevention remains easier than recovering from serious illness. Taking steps now can help individuals and families stay healthier throughout the months ahead while helping reduce the impact of seasonal viruses across the community. National physicians’ groups, including the American Academy of Pediatrics, issued immunization recommendations last week. The groups cited recent research from the Vaccine Integrity Project at the University of Minnesota and the American Medical Association published in the medical journal JAMA that found that the latest influenza, COVID-19 and respiratory syncytial virus vaccines remain safe and effective against severe illness. The groups said they are filling the need for a trusted source for vaccine recommendations as limited guidance is coming from the federal government. Pediatricians in Maine said the recommendations are important in keeping children safe as they start the new school year. “Parents are ready for their kids to come home with the runny noses and the coughs and all the things that come with going back to school,” said Dr. Kristy Perkowski, a pediatrician at the Northern Light Mercy Dr. Harry E. Davis Pediatric Center in Portland. Even healthy children that don’t have underlying medical conditions can face severe and potentially life-threatening complications from the viruses, she said, “and it’s for that reason that the American Academy of Pediatrics has maintained the vaccine schedule that we’ve been working with for some time and hasn’t changed the recommendations.” Typically, the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention would issue immunization guidelines this time of year, but the agency has so far not issued recommendations on COVID-19 or RSV shots and said health care providers should follow last year’s recommendations for the flu vaccine, citing “legal uncertainties and inquiries.” The agency’s advisory committee on immunization practices, a group of independent medical experts, has been in limbo since last year when Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. removed all committee members and replaced them with new members, including several vaccine skeptics. “There has been a complete dismantling of the system that we use to ensure that we provide safe care with the best evidence,” said Dr. Laura Blaisdell, a pediatrician and the co-chair of the Maine Immunization Coalition. The guidelines from the medical groups are meant to fill that gap, she said, and ensure “Americans have evidence-based recommendations without political bias.” This is the second year that the Vaccine Integrity Project has conducted a comprehensive review of scientific evidence on vaccine safety and effectiveness. The review found that the COVID-19, flu and RSV vaccines consistently reduced the risk of severe illness and hospitalization among various population groups, including children, pregnant individuals and older adults. The fall respiratory virus season typically starts in October and hits its peak in December and January. There were nearly 1,400 flu-related hospitalizations in Maine during the 2025-26 respiratory virus season, as well as 528 hospitalizations related to COVID-19 and 243 hospitalizations related to RSV, according to data from the Maine CDC. There were 73 deaths associated with the flu and 65 deaths related to COVID-19. Doctors in Maine have faced more questions from families about the safety of vaccines since the onset of the pandemic, as misinformation began to circulate, said Dr. Mary Ottolini, the chair of pediatrics at the MaineHealth Barbara Bush Children’s Hospital in Portland. “Everywhere, parents are understandably very confused,” she said. “The best thing parents can do to keep their children out of the hospital this winter is to get them vaccinated.” Here are the immunization recommendations issued last week by the American Academy of Pediatrics, American Academy of Family Physicians, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists and the Infectious Diseases Society of America: Influenza All children 6 months and older without underlying medical conditions should receive an annual flu vaccination, according to the groups’ recommendations. Children between the ages of 6 months and 8 years who have received fewer than two doses of the flu vaccine before July of this year or who have an unknown vaccine history should get two doses separated by at least four weeks. All other children 18 and younger should receive one dose of the vaccine. “As soon as it is available in your area, it’s appropriate to get it,” said Perkowski, the Portland pediatrician. “You want to get it before flu is circulating, before we’re hearing of an increase in cases and certainly by the end of October so that you are prepared for the peak of flu season.” All adults, including pregnant women, should receive an annual flu shot, per the groups’ guidance. COVID-19 All children under 2 years of age should receive an annual updated COVID-19 vaccination, according to the recommendations. Children 2 years and older who are at high risk of severe illness, live in group homes or live in households with people at high risk of severe illness should also get vaccinated. The pediatrics academy also said that any child two or older, regardless of risk factors, could get vaccinated if their parents wanted that. Although the group did not issue specific recommendations for those children, Perkowski said parents on the fence should consider that the vaccine is effective at reducing emergency room visits and hospitalizations related to COVID-19. “I always tell people there’s only so much we can do. There’s a lot of things we can protect against and some things we can’t,” Perkowski said. “And this is something where you can get additional protection.” The groups also recommend that all adults, including pregnant women, receive an annual updated COVID-19 vaccine. Adults 65 and older should receive two doses six months apart. Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) Women who are 32 to 36 weeks pregnant between September and March 1 should receive a dose of the RSV vaccine, per the groups’ guidance. Giving the vaccine during the last couple of months of pregnancy gives the body time to form antibodies and passes immunity to the baby. RSV is particularly dangerous to infants. The vaccine that is administered during pregnancy is relatively new to the market, and Ottolini, the pediatrics chair at the Barbara Bush Children’s Hospital, said doctors are already seeing the impact. “I can tell you it’s made a big difference in the number of babies that we are seeing who are hospitalized to begin with, and especially those who get really severely ill,” she said. Infants under 8 months of age whose mothers were not immunized during pregnancy should receive monoclonal antibodies during their first RSV season, according to the recommendations. Children 8 to 23 months old at high risk of severe illness and children under 18 who are immunocompromised should also receive a vaccine during RSV season. Adults between 50 and 74 who are at increased risk of severe illness should receive a one-time vaccination. All adults 75 and older should get the RSV vaccine. WHO prequalifies multi-dose vial of the maternal RSV vaccine, setting the stage for introduction September 11, 2026 by Tara Petronio Share: Facebook Bluesky LinkedIn Maternal, newborn, and child health With new WHO-prequalified products available, countries are poised to take next steps toward introducing maternal RSV vaccines and safeguarding infants from a major health threat. Staff at the Sendwe Hospital NICU in the Democratic Republic of the Congo care for newborn babies. Photo: PATH/Georgina Goodwin. Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is the leading cause of severe respiratory infections and hospitalizations in infants and young children. The virus is so widespread that nearly all children contract it before two years of age, but there are stark disparities in mortality: 98 percent of pediatric RSV deaths occur in low- and middle-income economies, where many children never make it to the hospital. In August 2026, the World Health Organization (WHO) prequalified the multi-dose vial presentation of maternal RSV vaccines, marking an important milestone on the path to broader introduction. Multi-dose vials can reduce storage, shipping, and packaging expenses while saving critical cold chain capacity, making them well suited for low- and middle-income markets. Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance has committed to opening a funding window for an RSV maternal immunization program, which will support introduction of the vaccine in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). With a product suitable for LMICs now available, now is the time for countries to begin exploring how they can introduce vaccines. Vaccinating mothers, protecting newborns The maternal RSV vaccine helps protect babies when they are the most vulnerable. Given in pregnancy, the vaccine enhances a pregnant woman’s immunity and increases natural antibody transfer to the baby for protection that lasts through the first critical months after birth. WHO globally recommends RSV vaccination in the third trimester of pregnancy, as defined by local guidelines. “RSV is a major cause of infant illness and death, especially in low-resource settings where some children never even reach care,” said Clint Pecenka, director of PATH’s RSV vaccine project. “Maternal vaccination offers a vital chance to reduce this burden—protecting babies early and easing the pressure on families and health systems.” RSV disease burden in low- and high-income contexts. Graphic: WHO; PATH; RRD. What RSV vaccines could mean for children The RSV maternal vaccine has shown impressive results in clinical trials. A Phase 3 clinical study found that protection from the vaccine remains high through 6 months after birth, with 82 percent efficacy in the first 90 days and 70 percent over 180 days. These data tell us that the vaccine can help protect children during their first 6 months of life, when RSV poses the greatest threat to their health. And real-world data from countries that have introduced the maternal RSV vaccine, like Argentina and Scotland, are emerging and showing high vaccine effectiveness, especially against severe disease. Further, RSV imposes a substantial strain on health systems and households, causing millions of hospitalizations and placing a burden on parents and caregivers. Introducing maternal vaccines could not only keep children out of the hospital, but could also avert health care costs and free up resources for other health priorities. “Our cost-of-delivery analyses in Kenya, Ghana, and Mozambique show that estimated costs of delivering new maternal vaccines such as for RSV are within the range of other routine childhood vaccine costs,” said Ranju Baral, a senior health economist at PATH. “Modeling studies also indicate that these vaccines can be cost-effective in many LMICs. In short, RSV vaccines are a smart investment in maternal and child health where needed most.” Turning readiness into reality With the multi-dose vial presentation of maternal RSV vaccines now prequalified, this is a key moment to prioritize planning for their roll out, especially given that RSV is a new disease target for many countries. As countries begin planning for RSV prevention, they’ll need to weigh the local impact of the disease, the cost and benefits of available products, and how well those products fit within their health systems. This process is already underway in some LMICs, and collaborative initiatives like the Maternal Immunization Readiness Network in Africa and Asia (MIRNA) are providing support. Other key steps will include preparing delivery platforms via antenatal care and immunization programs, raising awareness among health care providers and communities, and ensuring systems are ready to monitor safety and effectiveness. Long-term success will also depend on workforce readiness and securing funding. WHO, PATH, and other contributors have developed a suite of communications materials that cover RSV disease, new prevention tools, and delivery considerations. These tools can help support informed decision-making and implementation planning around RSV and relevant interventions. In addition, PATH’s RSV intervention cost calculator allows users to estimate costs of maternal RSV vaccine and mAb products available in the global market. Maternal RSV vaccines have exciting potential to protect infants from a deadly threat—one that has for too long been overlooked. By setting the stage for introduction, we can ensure that countries are well equipped to implement this lifesaving intervention in the coming years. content: A healthcare worker in Ghana prepares a vaccine for administration at a primary health clinic. Recent WHO prequalification of a multi-dose RSV vaccine aims to streamline delivery across low-resource settings. A new three-dose vial presentation of the maternal RSV vaccine received prequalification from the World Health Organization (WHO) on Wednesday, unlocking large-scale distribution across lower-income countries. The decision enables global health alliances to introduce affordable immunisation during pregnancy, protecting newborns from severe respiratory disease. Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) remains the second leading cause of infant mortality globally after malaria, claiming over 100,000 lives annually among children under five, according to the WHO. More than 97% of these deaths occur in low- and middle-income countries with a particularly high burden in sub-Saharan Africa, where healthcare facilities often lack specialised respiratory care. Pregnant women vaccinated in their third trimester with the multi-dose vial, marketed as Abrysvo by Pfizer , transfer protective antibodies across the placenta, shielding infants throughout their first six months of life. The vaccine showed high efficacy in global clinical trials across high- and low-income settings, according to the European Medicines Agency (EMA). In pivotal Phase 3 clinical trials, it demonstrated 81.8% efficacy against severe RSV-associated lower respiratory disease in the infant’s first 90 days, maintaining 69.4% efficacy through six months. Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, welcomed the WHO’s decision on Wednesday and announced it would expand access for lower-income countries. “The WHO prequalification of a multi-dose RSV maternal vaccine marks an important step towards ensuring that all children, regardless of where they are born, are protected at their very first breath,” said Emily Kobayashi, Director of Vaccine Programmes at Gavi. Expanding RSV vaccine access in low-income settings Building on Gavi’s board approval to establish a dedicated maternal programme for its 2026–2030 strategic period, the Vaccine Alliance said that eligible low-income countries can now apply for funding to integrate maternal immunisation into routine healthcare systems. The RSV vaccine was developed with support from the Gates Foundation and reduces logistical barriers and cold-chain costs for developing health systems by packing multiple doses into a single vial. While monoclonal antibodies offer direct passive protection to newborns, maternal vaccination provides an alternative route by conferring immunity before birth, broadening global prevention options alongside existing antibody therapies. Ensuring seamless rollout is critical. Even in high-income regions like Europe, implementation of RSV prevention has faced hurdles due to delivery gaps and fragmented funding – a challenge global health officials hope Gavi’s centralized support will prevent in lower-income settings. Monitoring safety and birth outcomes Regulatory bodies, including the EMA, authorised Abrysvo after concluding that its protective benefits far outweigh potential risks. Post-authorization surveillance in the United States confirmed that preterm birth rates among vaccinated mothers showed no statistically significant increase and remained within expected background levels. Routine post-marketing surveillance programmes in Europe and the United States continue to track real-world health outcomes to ensure standard safety monitoring across diverse populations. Advertisement Real-world data spanning 2 respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) seasons show adjuvanted RSVPreF3 vaccination (Arexvy) reduces the risk of RSV-related major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) exacerbations, and severe asthma exacerbations in adults 60 years and older.1,2 Ann Falsey, MD, professor of medicine at the University of Rochester School of Medicine, whose research focuses on clinical and translational studies of respiratory viral infections in adults, discussed the findings with HCPLive during the 2026 European Respiratory Society (ERS) Congress.1 Study Design: Two-Season Claims Data From the ERS Congress Late-Breaker The 2-season analysis was presented as a late-breaking oral presentation and an ePoster at the ERS Congress 2026 in Barcelona, Spain, extending 1-season findings GSK presented in February 2026 at RSVVW'26. The retrospective study used Optum Research Database claims data (August 2022-May 2025), comparing 662,982 vaccinated adults with 2,651,928 unvaccinated adults, matched and propensity-weighted for baseline balance. "They all dropped a little from season one to cumulative over season two, but to my way of thinking, they're in the same ballpark. You have to look at the confidence intervals, not just the point prevalence. These severe outcomes of major cardiovascular events, COPD exacerbations, and asthma exacerbations are, in my mind, all in the same range," Falsey said. Vaccine Effectiveness Holds Steady Across Outcomes in Season Two The 2-season analysis found VE of 58.5% against RSV-related MACE (95% CI, 46.0-68.1%), 57.6% against severe COPD exacerbations (95% CI, 46.1-66.7%), and 57.3% against severe asthma exacerbations (95% CI, 22.3-76.6%). These figures converge more tightly across outcomes than the season 1 data GSK presented at RSVVW'26, when VE measured 63.1%, 74.4%, and 61.6% for the same three endpoints. Falsey said similar protection against COPD and asthma exacerbations fits with RSV's tendency to trigger airway hyperreactivity regardless of the underlying obstructive disease. Interpreting Real-World Claims Data: Bias and Limitations Falsey noted comparisons of vaccinated and unvaccinated populations carry inherent risk of healthy user bias, since people who seek vaccination often engage in other health-protective behavior. Investigators addressed this using propensity score matching to balance the 2 cohorts, though Falsey cautioned some unmeasured bias can persist even with careful matching. Weighing Industry-Funded Real-World Evidence Against Randomized Trial Data The study was funded by GSK, with most coauthors employed by GSK or Optum. Falsey, an independent academic investigator, reviewed the data and interpretation. She said real-world evidence complements randomized trial data by capturing populations, such as immunocompromised and frail adults, generally excluded from clinical trials, along with infrequent endpoints such as hospitalization. When Might a Second Dose of Arexvy Make Sense? Falsey called revaccination timing purely conjectural but estimated a second dose might make sense around 3 to 4 years post-vaccination, depending on the threshold of protection against serious outcomes clinicians and patients find acceptable. The poster's authors noted the 2-season results may help inform future recommendations on revaccination timing. Editor’s note: Falsey reports institutional research support from AstraZeneca, BioFire Diagnostics, Janssen, Merck, Moderna, Pfizer, and Sanofi Pasteur, and personal/advisory fees from CyanVac, GSK, and Vax Co. content: Skip to main content Free news, local advertising, updated daily Founded 2009 September 15, 2026 BLUFFTON Home News Blanchard Valley Health System Bluffton Public Library Bluffton University Business Columnists Events Health Historical Bluffton Iconoclast View Letters Living in Bluffton Obituaries People Police/Fire/EMS Public Meetings Regional news Sports Worship Classifieds Calendar Advertisers Announcements Directory Display Ads Menus Contact Search form TUE Lions Club ● THU Bluffton Garden Club ● Community Meal ● CLICK for time & locations Hindsight is 20/20: Recent reports for RSV, flu, and COVID-19 Health / Sep 10, 2026 Email Copy Link By Karen Kier Pharmacist on behalf of the ONU HealthWise team The expression “hindsight is 20/20” is attributed to American humorist Richard Armour from an article in The Van Nuys News. The California newspaper was published on February 17, 1949. The term refers to the Snellen vision chart testing for visual acuity. The term is used to express a clearer vision of events after they have occurred. Vaccines can sometimes fit this category when we wonder how effective they may be in preventing or reducing disease. We are entering the fall/winter phase of flu, RSV, and COVID-19. September, October and November can be ideal months to consider getting vaccinated. Last flu season saw the emergence of a pretty nasty strain of influenza. The H3N2 subclade K mutation spread rapidly and caused a more severe form of the flu. The symptoms remained similar and included fever, cough, sore throat, body aches, headache, and chills. The H3N2 subclade K virus was responsible for a higher rate of hospitalization and death from the flu in 2025-2026. The 2026-2027 flu shots for this season all contain an H3N2 subclade K strain for improved protection. Actually, this year’s flu shots have all new strains for both the A and B subtypes. The egg-based flu vaccine contains subtype A H1N1 Missouri, subtype A H3N2 subclade K Darwin, and subtype B Tokyo Victoria lineage. The cell-based flu vaccine differs in the subtype B as the Pennsylvania strain from the Victoria lineage. The new mRNA flu vaccine (mFlusiva®) has the same H1N1 subtype, but the subtype A H3N2 subclade K is a Michigan strain from the Darwin lineage and the subtype B is the Pennsylvania strain. It is highly encouraged for those 6 months and older to get a flu vaccine this season. A new program allows the nasal flu vaccine (FluMist®) to be given at home through the FluMist® Home delivery program (www.flumist.com). FluMist® is a live attenuated vaccine and is only recommended for those ages 2 through 49 years. It can not be given to anyone with a suppressed immune system. You go to the website and answer medical questions and if you qualify, they will mail you the flu vaccine nasal spray for a $8.99 shipping and handling fee. The package is temperature controlled to maintain effectiveness. Ohio law allows home administration of FluMist® when sent from the company. For those over 65 years of age, the recommendation is to receive the flu vaccine considered to provide higher antibody response and this includes Fluzone® High-Dose, Flublok®, and Fluad®. For those over the age of 50 years, you may consider the new mRNA flu vaccine as an option. Study data in over 70,000 participants showed superior efficacy in preventing laboratory-confirmed flu when compared to the traditional flu vaccine. The mRNA flu vaccine was reported to be 26.6% more effective. In the 65-year-and-older group, the mRNA vaccine displayed a superior antibody response to traditional flu shots. Interestingly, the rate of side effects was similar between the mRNA vaccine and the traditional vaccine. Some individuals have had a concern due to side effects with the mRNA COVID-19 vaccine. It is important to note the difference with less side effects of the mRNA flu vaccine. Moderna has the only FDA-approved mRNA for the flu, but GSK has entered into research for their flu mRNA vaccine with clinical trials starting this fall. The RSV vaccine is for those 60 years of age and older and for those 50 years and older with risk factors for an increase in RSV infections, including lung disease and a suppressed immune system. The RSV vaccine is a one-and-done shot and should not be repeated unless advised by a healthcare professional. On May 28, 2026, the FDA announced that the COVID-19 vaccines needed to be updated with the SARS-CoV-2 JN.1-lineage XFG for the monovalent vaccines. This provides the best match for the current circulating COVID-19 viruses. The fall COVID-19 vaccines are in the process of being shipped to pharmacies and healthcare facilities in the next week. The 2026-2027 COVID-19 vaccines provide a different strain with better protection from infection. On September 2, 2026, the Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA) released special communications on the effectiveness and safety of the 2026-2027 flu, RSV and COVID-19 vaccines. A systematic review of 69 studies for the influenza vaccine showed a significant reduction in severe disease and hospitalizations, especially in older adults, infants, and children. For the RSV vaccine, the systematic review evaluated 75 studies and reported a reduced risk of severe RSV and hospitalizations in older adults, with a lower side effect profile than had previously been reported related to blood clots. In evaluating the COVID-19 systematic review, the authors evaluated 155 studies and concluded the vaccine for COVID-19 “consistently reduces the risk of hospitalizations” for those at high risk, including infants and pregnant women. The JAMA studies provide good 20/20 hindsight for the value of vaccines in flu, RSV and COVID-19. content: News Sports Entertainment Opinion Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals LOCAL What to know about this year’s flu, COVID-19 and RSV shots Emily Bader The Maine Monitor Sept. 15, 2026, 5:04 a.m. ET Doctors are encouraging Mainers to follow guidelines from major medical groups recommending regular annual vaccines ahead of the fall respiratory virus season. National physicians’ groups, including the American Academy of Pediatrics, issued immunization recommendations last week. The groups cited recent research from the Vaccine Integrity Project at the University of Minnesota and the American Medical Association published in the medical journal JAMA that found that the latest influenza, COVID-19 and respiratory syncytial virus vaccines remain safe and effective against severe illness. The groups said they are filling the need for a trusted source for vaccine recommendations as limited guidance is coming from the federal government. Pediatricians in Maine said the recommendations are important in keeping children safe as they start the new school year. “Parents are ready for their kids to come home with the runny noses and the coughs and all the things that come with going back to school,” said Dr. Kristy Perkowski, a pediatrician at the Northern Light Mercy Dr. Harry E. Davis Pediatric Center in Portland. Even healthy children that don’t have underlying medical conditions can face severe and potentially life-threatening complications from the viruses, she said, “and it’s for that reason that the American Academy of Pediatrics has maintained the vaccine schedule that we’ve been working with for some time and hasn’t changed the recommendations.” Typically, the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention would issue immunization guidelines this time of year, but the agency has so far not issued recommendations on COVID-19 or RSV shots and said health care providers should follow last year’s recommendations for the flu vaccine, citing “legal uncertainties and inquiries.” The agency’s advisory committee on immunization practices, a group of independent medical experts, has been in limbo since last year when Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. removed all committee members and replaced them with new members, including several vaccine skeptics. “There has been a complete dismantling of the system that we use to ensure that we provide safe care with the best evidence,” said Dr. Laura Blaisdell, a pediatrician and the co-chair of the Maine Immunization Coalition. The guidelines from the medical groups are meant to fill that gap, she said, and ensure “Americans have evidence-based recommendations without political bias.” This is the second year that the Vaccine Integrity Project has conducted a comprehensive review of scientific evidence on vaccine safety and effectiveness. The review found that the COVID-19, flu and RSV vaccines consistently reduced the risk of severe illness and hospitalization among various population groups, including children, pregnant individuals and older adults. The fall respiratory virus season typically starts in October and hits its peak in December and January. There were nearly 1,400 flu-related hospitalizations in Maine during the 2025-26 respiratory virus season, as well as 528 hospitalizations related to COVID-19 and 243 hospitalizations related to RSV, according to data from the Maine CDC. There were 73 deaths associated with the flu and 65 deaths related to COVID-19. Doctors in Maine have faced more questions from families about the safety of vaccines since the onset of the pandemic, as misinformation began to circulate, said Dr. Mary Ottolini, the chair of pediatrics at the MaineHealth Barbara Bush Children’s Hospital in Portland. “Everywhere, parents are understandably very confused,” she said. “The best thing parents can do to keep their children out of the hospital this winter is to get them vaccinated.” Here are the immunization recommendations issued last week by the American Academy of Pediatrics, American Academy of Family Physicians, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists and the Infectious Diseases Society of America: Influenza All children 6 months and older without underlying medical conditions should receive an annual flu vaccination, according to the groups’ recommendations. Children between the ages of 6 months and 8 years who have received fewer than two doses of the flu vaccine before July of this year or who have an unknown vaccine history should get two doses separated by at least four weeks. All other children 18 and younger should receive one dose of the vaccine. “As soon as it is available in your area, it’s appropriate to get it,” said Perkowski, the Portland pediatrician. “You want to get it before flu is circulating, before we’re hearing of an increase in cases and certainly by the end of October so that you are prepared for the peak of flu season.” All adults, including pregnant women, should receive an annual flu shot, per the groups’ guidance. COVID-19 All children under 2 years of age should receive an annual updated COVID-19 vaccination, according to the recommendations. Children 2 years and older who are at high risk of severe illness, live in group homes or live in households with people at high risk of severe illness should also get vaccinated. The pediatrics academy also said that any child two or older, regardless of risk factors, could get vaccinated if their parents wanted that. Although the group did not issue specific recommendations for those children, Perkowski said parents on the fence should consider that the vaccine is effective at reducing emergency room visits and hospitalizations related to COVID-19. “I always tell people there’s only so much we can do. There’s a lot of things we can protect against and some things we can’t,” Perkowski said. “And this is something where you can get additional protection.” The groups also recommend that all adults, including pregnant women, receive an annual updated COVID-19 vaccine. Adults 65 and older should receive two doses six months apart. Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) Women who are 32 to 36 weeks pregnant between September and March 1 should receive a dose of the RSV vaccine, per the groups’ guidance. Giving the vaccine during the last couple of months of pregnancy gives the body time to form antibodies and passes immunity to the baby. RSV is particularly dangerous to infants. The vaccine that is administered during pregnancy is relatively new to the market, and Ottolini, the pediatrics chair at the Barbara Bush Children’s Hospital, said doctors are already seeing the impact. “I can tell you it’s made a big difference in the number of babies that we are seeing who are hospitalized to begin with, and especially those who get really severely ill,” she said. Infants under 8 months of age whose mothers were not immunized during pregnancy should receive monoclonal antibodies during their first RSV season, according to the recommendations. Children 8 to 23 months old at high risk of severe illness and children under 18 who are immunocompromised should also receive a vaccine during RSV season. Adults between 50 and 74 who are at increased risk of severe illness should receive a one-time vaccination. All adults 75 and older should get the RSV vaccine. More CLINICAL QUESTION Do respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccines reduce RSV-associated respiratory tract illness in adults? Does vaccination of pregnant patients reduce RSV-associated respiratory tract illness in their infants? EVIDENCE-BASED ANSWER RSV vaccines reduce RSV-associated respiratory tract illness in older adults. RSV vaccination of pregnant patients reduces lower respiratory tract infections that require medical attention in their infants, including hospitalization due to RSV disease.1 (Strength of Recommendation: A, consistent, good-quality patient-oriented evidence.) PRACTICE POINTERS RSV is a prevalent and highly contagious cause of respiratory tract illness and accounts for approximately 2% of infant deaths worldwide.2 It also increases the risk of secondary otitis media and bacterial pneumonia and their sequelae in infants and children.3,4 RSV can cause severe respiratory tract disease in older adults, especially those with chronic cardiac and pulmonary disease.5 The authors of this Cochrane review sought to evaluate the risks and benefits of RSV vaccines, as well as their effect on RSV-related disease, hospitalization, and mortality. This Cochrane review included 14 randomized controlled trials with a total of 114,327 patients, most of whom were older adults (n = 99,931; mean age 68.1–69.5 years).1 Seven trials were conducted in the United States, and seven were international, including Europe, South America, Africa, and Asia. The trials evaluated five RSV vaccine formulations, including those not available in the United States. This summary focuses on results for clinically available vaccines approved by the US Food and Drug Administration, all of which target the prefusion protein. Notably, this review did not include monoclonal antibody injections (nirsevimab [Beyfortus] and clesrovimab [Enflonsia]), which are approved for infants in the United States. The authors considered vaccine effect on RSV illness frequency, hospitalization due to RSV illness, RSV-related mortality, and all-cause mortality.1 The follow-up in all studies was one RSV season. Harms were defined as serious adverse events related to vaccination (eg, neurologic disorders such as Guillain-Barré syndrome). Outcomes were primarily reported as vaccine efficacy (ie, the reduction in risk of disease-related events among vaccinated people compared with placebo). For example, a vaccine efficacy of 0.9 would indicate a 90% reduction in disease-related events in the vaccinated group. In older adults, the RSV vaccine reduced RSV-associated lower respiratory tract illness (vaccine efficacy = 0.77; 95% CI, 0.70–0.83) and acute respiratory illness (vaccine efficacy = 0.67; 95% CI, 0.60–0.73) but made little to no difference in all-cause mortality.1 Maternal vaccination reduced RSV-associated lower respiratory tract illness that required medical attention in infants (vaccine efficacy = 0.54; 95% CI, 0.28–0.71) and severe RSV-associated illness in infants (vaccine efficacy = 0.74; 95% CI, 0.44–0.88).1 Maternal vaccination also reduced infant hospitalization due to RSV-related illness (vaccine efficacy = 0.54; 95% CI, 0.27–0.71) but made little to no difference in RSV-associated infant mortality. Maternal vaccinations were administered between 24 and 36 weeks' gestation or 28 and 36 weeks' gestation. The review did not assess the effect of maternal vaccination timing on infant outcomes. Trials that involved older adults were significantly larger and more comprehensive than the others. Across all trials, vaccination resulted in no apparent increase in adverse events.1 The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends a single dose of RSV vaccine over a person's lifetime to prevent serious RSV infection in older adults (75 years or older) or adults aged 50 to 74 years at increased risk of severe disease.6 The CDC also recommends RSV vaccination for pregnant individuals between 32 and 36 weeks' gestation to prevent RSV infection in their infants.7 The practice recommendations in this activity are available at https://www.cochrane.org/CD016131​. content: RSV Vaccine Shows 100% Effectiveness in COPD: Jorgen Vestbo, MD A Danish cohort study found 100% RSV vaccine effectiveness in COPD, but Jorgen Vestbo, MD, urges caution interpreting real-world results. Captions are auto-generated. The results of a Danish cohort study assessing the effectiveness of the adjuvanted RSVPreF3 vaccine in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) were presented at the European Respiratory Society 2026 International Congress in Barcelona, Spain. The estimated vaccine effectiveness was 100% against RSV-related severe COPD exacerbation, RSV-coded hospitalizations, and RSV-related mortality, with no events observed among the fewer than 6000 vaccinated individuals in the study.1 Even so, these data should be interpreted with caution, Jorgen Vestbo, MD, a professor of respiratory medicine and an honorary consultant at the Northwest Lung Centre, Manchester University Hospital, and co-study author, said in an interview with The American Journal of Managed Care®. When outcome estimates are based on zero observed events, he explained, that alone calls for caution regardless of how the data were collected. Vestbo noted that a Danish health setting offers an advantage in capturing cases accurately, since infections are not registered based solely on a diagnosis code at discharge. "I don't know if you've seen, but there's another real-world study using the Optum database in the US, and of course, that's based on claims data, and either you have a claim diagnosis of RSV or not," he explained. "In the Danish system, you can actually go in and see if they were just coded as, for instance, a COPD exacerbation." He also said the Danish health system allows researchers to check patient microbiology databases to see whether a polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test for RSV came back positive or negative, giving them more confidence they are capturing more RSV infections. Still, he said, that does not remove the need for caution when the estimate is based on zero events. Generalizability From Trial to Real-World Practice Translating results from a controlled trial into real-world data is another area where researchers should proceed carefully, Vestbo said. While it may be reasonable to expect real-world findings to replicate a trial's results, researchers should also weigh generalizability and other external factors, such as the relatively uniform, largely Caucasian population studied in Denmark. "When you take in all the people that I would see in my clinic, it seems as if they will get the same benefit as they would if they had been in a trial, which is nice," Vestbo said. "I don't think you can say much more than that." References 1. Fonseca MJ, Bratkovic S, Colak Y, et al. Effectiveness of adjuvanted RSVPreF3 vaccine against severe exacerbations and mortality among patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: emerging results from a nationwide Danish cohort study. content: COVID hospitalizations are officially rising in NYC: Here is what to know about the ‘updated’ vaccines While the FDA has narrowed its primary guidance to seniors and high-risk groups, local health officials emphasize that climbing RSV numbers and alarming wastewater trends mean all New Yorkers should secure their free shots Paparacy / Shutterstock Save Natalia Alvarez · September 14, 2026 Add us as a preferred source The 19 best things to do with kids in NYC — overnight museum visits, decadent desserts, a bubble-filled planet, slimy fun, and more 41 Best Things To Do In NYC To Add To Your Bucket List According to recent state data, COVID-related hospitalizations are officially on the rise across the five boroughs. Between August 30 and September 5, the city recorded more than 500 hospital admissions—the highest weekly count we’ve seen since early October of last year. What the latest NYC health data shows While overall COVID levels remain lower than in years past, confirmed cases and wastewater surveillance both show a clear upward trend. Health officials also unfortunately reported 12 COVID-related deaths during the first week of September. On top of that, city data shows that emergency room visits for RSV (respiratory syncytial virus) are beginning to climb, while flu cases currently remain flat. Who should get the new ‘updated’ vaccines? To keep the city healthy, state and city health officials are heavily endorsing a comprehensive slate of vaccine recommendations backed by major medical groups like the American Academy of Pediatrics. While the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved updated COVID vaccines in late August with a narrow recommendation for people over 65 or those with high-risk health conditions, New York City’s guidance is much broader. Powered By 10 Sec 26.6K 1 Next Stay Here is what local health experts are currently recommending for New Yorkers: All adults: Broadly encouraged to get the updated COVID-19 shots, which explicitly includes people who are pregnant. Young children: Vaccination is recommended for all children between 6 months and 2 years old, plus any older children with high-risk health conditions or whose parents simply want them vaccinated. Flu and RSV: An annual flu shot is recommended for everyone over 6 months old. RSV vaccinations are advised for older adults and infants. Promenade Pix / Shutterstock Where to find your shots (and skip the red tape) Booking an appointment is also relatively hurdle-free at major pharmacies: CVS: The online scheduler currently does not ask patients to verify underlying medical conditions. Walgreens: While their system asks patients to self-attest that they are “at high risk,” they are not requiring a prescription or physical proof to book. If you are looking to get vaccinated ahead of the fall rush, New Yorkers can easily find the closest clinic or pharmacy by using the city’s official map of vaccine providers. Vaccinating pregnant people in the third trimester protects their newborns against RSV infection and reduces a baby’s risk of being hospitalized with the virus by more than 80%. Vaccines need the WHO’s seal of approval before United Nations agencies such as UNICEF can buy them to distribute to lower-income countries. Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, agreed last year to fund the introduction of maternal RSV vaccination in multiple countries, and has been working to lay the groundwork for its rollout. Although the WHO prequalified single-dose vials in 2025, Gavi’s maternal RSV vaccination program could not begin until the agency prequalified multi-dose vials, which reduce the cost and difficulty of mass immunizations. Benefits of multi-dose vials Multi-dose vials allow healthcare professionals to vaccinate more people, but take up less storage space on delivery trucks or in clinics. Multi-dose products also make it easier to maintain a “cold chain,” in which vaccines are refrigerated at an appropriate temperature on the journey from the factory into people’s arms. RSV hospitalizes 3.6 million and kills 100,000 children under age five years each year, according to the WHO. Newborns are especially vulnerable. Pfizer released the maternal RSV vaccine, Abrysvo, in the United States in 2023. The Gates Foundation provided funding to develop a multi-dose version. Getting the multi-dose product prequalified “is a key milestone for RSV and, more broadly, for pneumonia prevention and reducing infant mortality globally,” said Ignacio Esteban, Gavi’s senior policy manager and incoming head of the adult and adolescent vaccines portfolio. CDC adds 1,150 more Cyclospora cases to US total In other food outbreak news, yesterday the CDC added 1,150 Cyclospora cases to the US total, lifting the caseload to 19,595 infections. The clinic is made possible through the Salt Lake County Health Department, Division of Services of the Deaf and Hard of Hearing, and Workforce Services Rehabilitation. Kristin Murphy, Deseret News By Lois M. Collins Lois is a longtime Deseret News special projects and family issues reporter, including health, parenting, aging and policy. Why now: The CDC's advisory panel, ACIP, is in legal limbo after Kennedy fired its members and a judge blocked the replacements, creating a vacuum these medical groups are filling independently. Coverage and pharmacy dispensing rules vary by state, creating a patchwork that may affect who can get vaccinated where. Just in time for updated flu, COVID-19 and RSV vaccines to hit pharmacies and doctors’ offices ahead of respiratory illness season, a number of leading medical groups have published their recommendations for who needs to have a vaccine. The fall and winter respiratory virus season typically runs October through the middle of May. Their advice, which was published in JAMA , the Journal of the American Medical Association, differs somewhat from the official guidance from the Trump administration, which came out at the end of August. The medical groups said they formed their recommendations after a careful examination of the latest evidence. The American Medical Association teamed up with the Vaccine Integrity Project at the University of Minnesota to lead the consortium, which included reviews and buy-in on specific relevant recommendations by several groups: the American Academy of Pediatrics for guidance on vaccines for minors, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists regarding vaccines during pregnancy, the Infectious Diseases Society of America for immunocompromised people and the American Academy of Family Physicians for adults and healthcare providers. They each published the guidance by subgroup separately, as well. In a media briefing, Dr. Bruce Gellin, board chairman for the Vaccine Integrity Project, said the move was necessary because “unfortunately, today the federal government is not fulfilling that responsibility in the way that it historically has, but the need for the work has not disappeared.” A chaotic time in vaccine history An influenza vaccine is pictured at a free vaccine clinic at the Sanderson Community Center in Taylorsville on Wednesday, Nov. 9, 2022. The clinic is made possible through the Salt Lake County Health Department, Division of Services of the Deaf and Hard of Hearing, and Workforce Services Rehabilitation. | Kristin Murphy, Deseret News The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has a panel that is charged with making recommendations on vaccines, but that hasn’t happened because of legal issues. As Deseret News has reported, the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices panel was fired last year and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. selected seven new members, adding several others after that. Then a federal judge said he couldn’t do that and temporarily suspended their appointments and vacated their actions. The panel itself is in limbo, so no new recommendations have been made by it this year. The judge also put on hold the guidance that those not on the approved list who want a vaccine have to talk to a healthcare provider. Many, including health experts, call the situation confusing. It’s worth noting that doctors can administer the shots off-label. But without new ACIP recommendations, the federal flu guidance remains the same as last year’s . For COVID-19 The collaborative has recommended the updated COVID-19 vaccine for all adults, with no carve-out for pregnancy or breastfeeding. Those older than 65 or who are immunocompromised should get a second dose. For children, the groups suggest each child from 6 to 23 months old be vaccinated, as well as children 2 and older who have underlying medical conditions. They don’t take a position on children over 2, but Dr. James Campbell, chairman of the American Academy of Pediatrics’ infectious disease committee, told The New York Times it is appropriate if a parent wants the child to have it. The medical groups note that the shots reduced the need for hospitalization or serious health impacts from the viral illness. They also noted no new safety concerns and said that, while possible, serious side effects are extremely uncommon, the benefits outweighing the risk for most people. But as Deseret News wrote a few weeks ago, there are variations in terms of insurance coverage and state regulations regarding dispensing vaccines. “Most people head to local pharmacies for their COVID shots. And not all doctors have the vaccines on hand. Whether pharmacies will choose to administer shots off-label — or even whether their states allow it — could vary widely nationwide.” No official federal advice has been given for COVID-19 shots, although the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved the COVID-19 vaccines only for adults over 65 or those with a medical condition that might make them high risk. Others can get the vaccine after consulting their physician, who can administer the shots as he or she sees fit. What about flu? As for flu, the review of research found that vaccination reduces risk of serious illness. And the guidance is simple: Everyone 6 months and older should be vaccinated and for the best coverage. The best time to get the vaccine in terms of protection from influenza, per the groups, is by the end of October. Per the CDC, “While vaccination by the end of October is recommended, vaccination should continue after October and throughout the influenza season as long as influenza viruses are circulating and unexpired vaccine is available.” The CDC specifically urges the seasonal flu vaccine for those at high risk of complications or severe illness — and it’s a long list that includes children 6 months old to 5 years, anyone 50 and older, those with chronic conditions, those with weakened immune systems, women who are or will be pregnant in flu season, children and adolescents on certain medications who could experience Reye syndrome after an influenza infection, those in nursing homes or long-term care facilities, American Indian or Alaska Native people, and those with extreme obesity. 5 Comments The FDA approved an mRNA flu vaccine — the first of its kind — for adults 50 and older in August. Healthline noted that in a clinical trial enrolling 40,703 adults 50 and older, people who received the mRNA vaccine had about 26% fewer cases of lab-confirmed flu-like illness than people who received a standard-dose shot,” based on the JAMA influenza review. Respiratory syncytial virus The federal government has thus far been silent on RSV guidance for the upcoming season. But the medical-group collaborative said that adults 75 and older need a one-time RSV vaccine, as do those 50 to 74 who are at increased risk, according to the medical groups. Immunocompromised adults and adolescents should also be vaccinated, with the number and frequency of doses decided case by case, per the Times. Women who are in their last trimester between September and March 1 are urged to get the vaccine so that their babies will be protected during RSV season, since RSV is very hard on infants. And if mom isn’t vaccinated while pregnant, infants under 8 months old should be given monoclonal antibodies. As for older infants, those 8 to 19 months at higher risk should be vaccinated their second season, whether they had a previous vaccination or not. Join the Conversation Looking for comments? Medical professionals recommend a flu vaccine for protection.(WLOX) By WAND Digital Staff Published: Sep. 11, 2026 at 12:31 PM UTC Share Add Us On GoogleAdd as a preferred source on Google SPRINGFIELD, Ill. (WAND) – The Illinois Department of Public Health has released its fall immunization guidance for flu, RSV and COVID-19 ahead of the 2026-27 respiratory virus season. The guidance was developed with recommendations from the Illinois Immunization Advisory Committee, a group of health experts. IDPH said the recommendations are intended to give residents and health care providers science-based information about vaccines. IDPH recommends flu vaccination for everyone 6 months and older. For RSV, the agency recommends vaccination for pregnant people between 32 and 36 weeks of pregnancy if they have not previously been vaccinated. The maternal RSV vaccine season runs from September through March 1. RSV immunization is also recommended for infants younger than 8 months without maternal vaccine protection entering their first RSV season, certain children ages 8 months through 19 months at increased risk of severe illness, adults ages 50 through 74 at increased risk and adults 75 and older if they have not previously been vaccinated. IDPH recommends COVID-19 vaccination for children ages 6 months through 23 months; children ages 2 through 18 in certain risk groups or if desired; pregnant, postpartum or breastfeeding people and those planning pregnancy; and all adults 19 and older. The department also issued a standing order allowing COVID-19 vaccines to be offered at additional locations, an effort officials said is meant to reduce barriers to vaccination. IDPH Director Dr. Sameer Vohra encouraged residents to stay current on recommended immunizations to lower their risk of serious illness. content: Did you know that thousands of children under the age of 5 are hospitalized each year with flu complications, and that about 90% of those youngsters aren't vaccinated? That's according to the American Academy of Pediatrics, which recommends an annual influenza vaccine for all children 6 months of age and older. Essentia Health is making it easier than ever for people to protect themselves against the flu and other viruses this respiratory season. Options include: Vaccine clinics and events : These walk-in opportunities are held at Essentia clinics, pharmacies or during special events. Visit our Getting Your Vaccines webpage to find a schedule of upcoming vaccine clinics, where patients can receive vaccines for flu, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), COVID-19 (once available) and other illnesses. You don't need to be an Essentia patient to attend one of these clinics. : These walk-in opportunities are held at Essentia clinics, pharmacies or during special events. "Vaccines remain one of the most effective tools we have to prevent severe illness, hospitalization and complications from respiratory viruses," said Dr. Dhilhan Marasinghe, a pediatrician at Essentia Health. "By getting vaccinated before the season ramps up, you’re not only protecting yourself — you’re also helping protect family members, coworkers and others in the community who may be more vulnerable." Please note that the availability of COVID-19 vaccine will vary by Essentia Health location. Some locations will start offering COVID vaccine as soon as this week, while others won't start until later this month or early October. Contact your clinic or pharmacy ahead of time to learn more. content_title: 在VNVC疫苗接种系统正式推出RSV单克隆抗体。
content: Tiếng Việt 首页 话题 时事 政治制度 当地的 事件 旅游 快乐越南 企业 产品 遗产 博物馆 数字 多媒体 数据 Văn hóa - Xã hội 医疗的 在VNVC疫苗接种系统正式推出RSV单克隆抗体。 (丹治报)——越南儿童首次在250多个越南国家疫苗接种中心接种单克隆抗体,以预防由呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)引起的肺炎和毛细支气管炎,即使在呼吸道疾病爆发高峰期,也满足了有效且低成本的疾病预防需求。 Báo Dân trí•24/12/2025 Google Google 0 单克隆抗体在越南正式获准使用仅两个月后,越南国家疫苗接种中心(VNVC)便成为首个部署呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)单克隆抗体疫苗的疫苗接种中心。此次部署遵循了卫生部疾病预防司于12月22日发布的专业指南。 此次事件标志着 RSV 早期预防策略向前迈出了一步,从治疗机构扩展到专业的全国性疫苗接种系统,迅速满足了主动预防的需求,并有助于降低 RSV 引起的治疗和住院费用。 在越南国家兽医中心(VNVC)启动呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)单克隆抗体预防项目的第一天, 来自河内市祥梅坊的阮翠琼女士(31岁)就带着她6个多月大的女儿来到VNVC长征医院进行预防性检查。她说,女儿2个月大的时候就患过毛细支气管炎,不得不住院治疗,导致她和丈夫轮流请假照顾女儿。 Khám phá thêm Khám Phá Tour Dịch Từ Điển du lịch 来自河内的阮翠琼女士是每年呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)高发期首批带孩子到越南国家疫苗接种中心(VNVC)接种单克隆抗体疫苗的家长之一(照片:Le Anh Tuan)。 “当我得知越南国家疫苗中心(VNVC)提供预防呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)的单克隆抗体疫苗时,我立即带孩子去接种了疫苗。及早采取预防措施让我更加安心;如果我的孩子真的生病了,病情也会比较轻微,对我的孩子和我的家人来说压力也会更小,”琼女士分享道。 胡志明市谭英综合医院新生儿中心主任甘玉芳医生指出,呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)是全球婴幼儿住院的主要原因。该病毒很容易通过呼吸道传播,与普通感冒类似。 然而,感染呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)的儿童可能出现急性呼吸衰竭、肺不张、细菌继发感染、气胸、脱水、心律失常、呼吸骤停甚至死亡。此外,该疾病还可能留下长期后遗症,例如肺纤维化、呼吸功能障碍、再次住院或慢性哮喘。 方医生指出,呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)是儿童毛细支气管炎病例的50%至90%以及肺炎病例的5%至40%的病因。高达75%至90%的儿童在出生第一年内会感染RSV,其中0.5%至2%需要住院治疗,这意味着每100名感染RSV的儿童中,大约有0.5至2名需要住院治疗。 “VNVC疫苗接种系统扩大单克隆抗体的使用范围,使家长更容易及早为孩子接种疫苗并主动预防疾病,尤其是在RSV感染和严重并发症的高风险时期。这不仅降低了高峰期的住院率和治疗机构的压力,还有助于家庭节省费用和就医时间,并降低儿童出现长期后遗症的风险,”Phuong博士评论道。 12月23日上午,Van Chi Linh 女士带着她两个多月大的儿子 Gia Hung 来到胡志明市的 VNVC Le Dai Hanh 接受单克隆抗体注射,以预防 RSV 感染。(照片:Diem Chinh) VNVC疫苗系统医疗主任白氏征博士表示,RSV单克隆抗体采用重组生物技术生产,可直接提供特异性抗体,帮助儿童在接种疫苗后立即获得保护,而无需像其他疫苗那样等待身体产生免疫力。 12个月以下的婴儿只需接种一剂,12至24个月大且呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)感染风险较高的儿童也可接种。该抗体疫苗可在出生后立即接种,适用于所有新生儿,包括早产儿、低出生体重儿或患有基础疾病的新生儿,安全性良好,接种后不良反应报告较少。 VNVC 正在尽一切努力,使用严格遵守国际标准的专用冷藏车系统,尽快将单克隆抗体运送到全国各地的中心(照片:Moc Thao)。 “研究表明,该产品可将因呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)感染而住院和需要重症监护的风险降低82%以上,且保护作用至少持续5-6个月。截至10月,这种RSV单克隆抗体已在近60个国家获得批准,包括美国、法国、英国、加拿大、 日本和澳大利亚,并已被25个以上发达国家纳入国家免疫规划,” Chinh博士介绍道。 VNVC推出单克隆抗体,并与Nutrihome诊所合作,从11月开始实施(照片:An Nhien)。 此前,越南国家疫苗接种中心(VNVC)于 10 月在 Tam Anh 综合医院系统和 Nutrihome 诊所(同一医疗生态系统内的单位)启动并实施了 RSV 单克隆抗体疫苗接种,并得到了医生和许多有幼儿的家长的积极反馈。 除了 RSV 单克隆抗体外,VNVC 还分别于 9 月底和 12 月 14 日推出了辉瑞的 RSV 疫苗和葛兰素史克的新技术 RSV 疫苗,在呼吸道疾病增加的情况下,为高危人群提供了及时的保护。 持续向婴幼儿推广抗 RSV 单克隆抗体,帮助 VNVC 完成了 RSV 预防方案的“三重”组合,从而形成预防严重肺炎并发症、毛细支气管炎和呼吸衰竭的生命周期策略,保护从儿童和孕妇到老年人和有基础疾病的所有年龄段人群。 (Baohatinh.vn)——河静省总医院的医生警告说,呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)引起的症状如咳嗽、流鼻涕和发烧,如果不及时治疗,可能会发展为毛细支气管炎、肺炎和呼吸衰竭。 Báo Hà Tĩnh • 12/09/2026 病例数量迅速增加 近日,前往 河静 省总医院儿科就诊的呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)感染患儿数量不断增加。其中许多患儿因家人在家自行用药而出现严重症状入院。 患者阮福阮得到了医生的悉心照料和治疗,病情有所好转。 一个典型的例子是阮福阮(Nguyen Phuc Nguyen,5个月大,奇英乡)的病例。他出现咳嗽、流鼻涕和低烧等症状。家人以为只是普通的呼吸道疾病,便在家积极观察和照顾孩子。然而,大约3天后,孩子的病情没有好转;咳嗽加剧,出现喘息,呼吸急促,食欲下降。家人察觉到异常,便带孩子去省立综合医院就诊。经过检查和基本检测,孩子被确诊为呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)感染。 Khám phá thêm Dịch Từ Điển Ghé Điểm Đến Học Làm Bánh 患者阮福阮的母亲阮氏玉女士分享道:“当医生宣布我儿子呼吸道合胞病毒检测呈阳性时,我们全家都非常担心,因为他最初只有咳嗽、流鼻涕和发烧的症状,所以我们以为他只是普通感冒。入院接受医生治疗和观察后,他的咳嗽和喘息症状有所缓解,食欲也改善了,我们全家这才放心了不少。” 来自东田乡的何氏芳女士的孩子,在省总医院儿科接受了一周多的治疗后,现在已经可以出院了。“我的孩子出生才12天就出现了咳嗽、流鼻涕和发烧的症状。家人赶紧带他去医院检查治疗。因为他太小了,医生诊断他感染了呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV),我们全家都很担心。但是,多亏了医生们的悉心照料和治疗,他的症状逐渐消退,现在已经可以出院了。”芳女士说道。 最近,儿科感染呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)的患者人数有所增加。 这是省立总医院儿科目前正在照护和治疗的数十名呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)感染患者中的两名。该科室平均每天接收10-12例RSV检测呈阳性的病例,其中一些患者会发展为毛细支气管炎或肺炎,需要密切监测。 省立综合医院儿科副主任杨文甲医生表示:“呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)是婴幼儿呼吸道感染的常见病因之一。该病通常以流鼻涕、咳嗽、发烧、乏力、食欲不振等症状开始。当病毒深入下呼吸道时,患儿可能出现毛细支气管炎、肺炎,甚至呼吸衰竭。RSV感染患儿出现严重并发症的风险各不相同。新生儿、早产儿、低出生体重儿以及患有基础心脏、肺部或免疫缺陷疾病的患儿发生并发症的风险更高。因此,当这些人群的孩子出现呼吸道症状时,家长更需格外警惕。” 省立总医院儿科副主任杨文甲医生正在检查一名感染呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)的患者。 需要注意的是,目前尚无针对呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)的特效疗法。治疗主要侧重于控制症状、支持呼吸、确保充足的营养、维持体液平衡以及监测患儿病情。因此,早期发现和及时 就医 至关重要,尤其是在患儿病情出现恶化迹象时。 为应对呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)感染儿童数量的增加,河静省总医院儿科正在加强感染控制措施,对患者进行分类和监测,并严格执行院内交叉感染预防措施。此举旨在降低病毒在儿科患者,特别是免疫系统较弱的幼儿中的传播风险。 积极预防疾病并及早识别严重症状。 呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)主要通过呼吸道飞沫和直接接触感染者的分泌物传播。当儿童与感染者密切接触时,例如通过咳嗽、打喷嚏或接触被病毒污染的物体表面,再触摸眼睛、鼻子或嘴巴,病​​毒就可能传播。在家庭、学校和托儿所等儿童经常密切接触的环境中,感染风险更高。因此,随着呼吸道疾病病例的增加,主动限制感染源是保护儿童的关键措施。 医生建议,当儿童出现异常症状,特别是呼吸困难或发烧时,应带他们到医疗机构进行检查。 河静省卫生厅建议,为预防呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)和其他呼吸道疾病,家长应从孕期开始重视孩子的健康。孕妇需要接受充分的产前护理,确保胎儿足月出生,体重健康,并具备良好的健康基础。 此外,家庭需要保持清洁通风的居住环境;定期清洗孩子的手、鼻子、喉咙和身体;并清洁孩子经常接触的物品和玩具。照护者在接触、照护或喂食孩子之前,也应使用肥皂或消毒液洗手。 省立总医院儿科副主任杨文甲医生强调:“当儿童出现呼吸道疾病症状时,应尽量减少带他们去人多的地方,并避免与咳嗽、发烧、流鼻涕或患有其他呼吸道疾病的人密切接触。家长切勿在没有医生处方的情况下自行给孩子用药,尤其是抗生素。自行用药或在家疏于观察会导致病情恶化,而无法及时发现。” 如果呼吸道合胞病毒感染没有被及时发现和治疗,可能会引起许多危险的并发症,尤其是在幼儿和婴儿中。
